## Defect list

### 1. Webinar attendance → retention

**a. Correlation treated as causation.** Attendance wasn't randomly assigned. Customers who choose to sign up for and attend an optional webinar are almost certainly more engaged, more invested in the product, or earlier adopters than those who skip it — any of which independently predicts staying on the plan. The 31% gap could be entirely explained by this self-selection, with the webinar itself doing nothing. *Effect:* the causal claim ("webinars therefore cause higher retention") is unsupported by the data actually shown.

**b. Sample is restricted to survivors.** The comparison is built entirely from the 412 customers who are *still active* — churned customers aren't in the analysis at all. That's selecting on the outcome you're trying to explain. It also confounds attendance with tenure: customers who have stuck around longer have simply had more chances to attend a webinar, which can manufacture a spurious attendance–retention link even if webinars have zero effect. *Effect:* the 31% figure may not reflect webinars' relationship to churn at all, and could even reverse under a proper cohort (attend vs. not, tracked forward, including people who left).

**c. Extrapolation from voluntary to mandatory.** Even granting the correlation, the mechanism plausibly driving it is the customer's own motivation to opt in — not the webinar content itself. Making attendance mandatory removes exactly that self-selection, so there's no basis for assuming forced attendees will show the same 31% gap. *Effect:* the policy recommendation (mandatory webinars for all new customers) may deliver no retention benefit even if the original observation is entirely real.

### 2. Central region and churn

**d. Multiple-comparisons problem / p-hacking.** 18 attributes were tested against churn, and the one that cleared p < 0.05 is being reported as a finding. With 18 independent tests at α = 0.05, you'd expect roughly one "significant" result to turn up by chance alone even if none of the attributes actually matter. A p = 0.04 result plucked from 18 tries, with no correction (e.g., Bonferroni would demand roughly p < 0.003), is statistically indistinguishable from noise. *Effect:* the Central-region effect is likely a false positive, and resources get redirected based on what may be a random fluctuation in the data.

**e. Recommendation doesn't follow even if the finding is real.** The memo moves from "Central churns least" to "spend more in Central" without establishing why that follows. Correlation between region and churn doesn't identify a lever spend can pull, and there's no argument for why reinforcing an already-strong region beats addressing high-churn regions where there's more room for improvement (or investigating *why* Central retains well and replicating that elsewhere). *Effect:* budget gets allocated on a non sequitur — the data, even taken at face value, doesn't say that spending in Central produces any additional return.

### 3. Satisfaction increase and the support model

**f. Pre/post comparison with no control, causally attributed.** A rise from 62% to 66% across one quarter is attributed entirely to the new support model, but nothing rules out seasonality, other initiatives launched in the same window, changes in the survey population or method, or plain regression to the mean. There's no counterfactual (e.g., a comparison group that didn't get the new model). *Effect:* credit is assigned to the support model on the basis of a coincidence-in-time, not evidence of a causal link — the "it's working" conclusion is asserted, not demonstrated.

**g. No indication the 4-point move is meaningful rather than noise.** No confidence interval, sample size, or significance test is given for the satisfaction score itself, so there's no way to tell whether 62%→66% reflects a real shift or ordinary survey-to-survey variation. *Effect:* a change that may be within normal noise is being treated as a confirmed, actionable signal.
